items.title: Trade and AI Were Said Out Loud at the Trump–Xi Summit. Taiwan Wasn't.
items.body: At the high-profile summit in Washington between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping, Deutsche Welle reports, there was much talk of trade and artificial intelligence. One of the most contentious issues, Taiwan, was discussed only in private, according to the same report television piece drinking from the same reporting adds nothing beyond the source's own framing awaiting evidence it does not contain — omit such filler and speak to the arrangement itself).

sources.title: Montreal squirrels change their coat colour depending on neighbourhood they live in, new study finds

discussion.body: A neighbourhood pattern isn't the same as watching an animal change. The finding describes colour varying across areas, not individual squirrels switching coats after a move.
Fair — but it does point at which conditions might be doing the work, since temperature and forest cover are the factors named.

items.title: Montreal's Eastern Grey Squirrels Vary in Coat Colour by Neighbourhood
items.body:
A new McGill study found that eastern grey squirrels in Montreal vary in coat colour depending on the neighbourhood they live in, CBC reports. The reported driver is local environment: the animals are influenced by conditions that include temperature and forest cover.

The interesting implication is scale. If heat and tree canopy shift from block to block, a city becomes a patchwork of slightly different habitats, and the squirrels' coats appear to track that patchwork rather than the city as a whole.

sources.title: Photos: These shepherds climb down a mountain to go to night school

items.title: The Schools Teaching Lesotho's Herders Their ABCs
items.body: Herding is a vital profession in Lesotho, and it comes with a cost: many thousands of boys and men who take it up have to give up their education, NPR reports. A small network of schools, run on a shoestring budget, is trying to give some of that back by teaching them the ABCs.

sources.title: ‘Jack & Christine’ Trailer: John Hawkes Turns A Dinner Party Into A Night of Chaos – Film News in Brief

items.title: John Hawkes Is the Guest Who Ruins Dinner in the 'Jack & Christine' Trailer
items.body:
"Jack & Christine," a thriller short starring John Hawkes, has released its first trailer ahead of a world premiere at Beyond Fest on Sunday. The trailer shows married couple Jack (Luke Barnett) and Christine (Nikki Lorenzo) hosting a dinner party that suddenly spirals into an intense, chaotic evening when a guest played by Hawkes turns up.

The dinner-party-gone-wrong remains one of film's most economical setups: one table, a handful of people, and a single arrival that detonates the room. Casting Hawkes as the arrival is doing a lot of the marketing work here.

sources.title: Jia Zhangke Readies Zhao Tao Road Movie ‘Mamma Dunhuang,’ Rules Out AI in Production (EXCLUSIVE)

items.title: Jia Zhangke's Next Feature Is a Road Movie Called 'Mamma Dunhuang'
items.body: Jia Zhangke will move on to location scouting and production design for his next film, the road movie "Mamma Dunhuang," once the 10th Pingyao Crouching Tiger Hidden Dragon International Film Festival wraps on Sept. 30, Variety reports. The film follows a woman who drives from Dunhuang, in western China near Central Asia.

sources.title: Heathrow Airport warns third runway could be delayed by four years

discussion.body: It's the airport itself flagging the slip, which is a strange kind of warning coming from the party that wants to build the thing.
Or a realistic one. An operator living with its own construction timetables has better information than a minister defending a date announced years earlier.

items.title: Heathrow Warns Its Third Runway May Slip Four Years Past the 2035 Target
items.body: The UK's busiest airport says its third runway could be delayed by four years, cautioning that it may miss the government target of 2035. Ministers, for their part, say the deadline has always been ambitious — a hedge that arrived well before the miss it describes.

sources.title: Ina Garten Explains Why She’s “Always Said No” To A Biopic: “It’s My Story”

discussion.body: A memoir is the version you control; a film is the version someone else makes. Declining is a coherent position, not a lack of nerve.
Distance isn't automatically betrayal, though. Someone who didn't live inside the story may notice things the memoirist couldn't.

items.title: Ina Garten Keeps Saying No to the Biopic Treatment
items.body: Ina Garten already told her own story in her 2024 memoir, Be Ready When the Luck Happens. She is now reluctant to trust a filmmaker with it: despite being approached to adapt the book for the big screen, she has explained that she has never been willing to make a biopic about her life. The stated reason is ownership — the story is hers.

sources.title: Film Execs Ponder Federal Film Tax Credit Impact, Timeline & Potential Price Rises — Zurich Summit

items.title: A 20% Federal Film Incentive Bill, and Financiers Sizing Up the Prospects
items.body: Last week a bipartisan group of lawmakers unveiled a bill for a 20% federal film incentive, which with bonuses could bring the total rebate to 30%. At the Zurich Summit this weekend, a group of film financiers were asked for their thoughts on the prospects of a US federal film incentive — the mechanism now exists on paper; what it does to the business is the open question.

sources.title: Playing 'La Bamba' for an hour? Must be a Mexican fandango!

items.title: A 300-Year-Old Fandango Tradition, Revived One All-Nighter at a Time
items.body: A 300-year-old Mexican musical tradition is finding new life around the world, NPR reports — one all-night fandango at a time. The gatherings described are sweaty and joyous, and they run until morning.

sources.title: Killer Christa Pike is to be executed within days but her defence say she's a victim too

discussion.body: The claim turns on the sentencing regime, not on the act: same crime, different era, different outcome. That is a cleaner argument than a plea for sympathy, and a harder one to answer.

Cleaner, but narrower. A hypothetical sentence from a court today doesn't by itself settle whether this particular defendant should be spared — the clemency request needs a second step that the reported claim doesn't take.

items.title: Pike's Lawyers Argue a 1995 Killing Wouldn't Bring a Death Sentence Now
items.body: Lawyers for Christa Pike, who killed a fellow student in 1995, argue she should get clemency and that she would not be sentenced to death if the crime happened today, the BBC reports. The point is about time as much as about her: the same act, weighed against the standards a court would apply now rather than then.

sources.title: Pope Leo draws 800,000 people to central Paris for open-air Mass on iconic square

discussion.body: Influence and observance are not the same variable. A single gathering shows reach on an afternoon; the pews show habit, and habit is the thing the church is losing.
Fair, but a crowd that still assembles is not nothing either. An institution that can draw a mass turnout retains a kind of cultural standing, even in a country where attendance is falling.

items.title: A Papal Crowd in Paris and the Empty Pews Across Europe
items.body: The crowd that turned out for Pope Leo's open-air Mass in central Paris testified, in PBS's reading, to the church's lasting influence in France — set against declining attendance and the secularisation that has emptied churches across Europe. Those are two different kinds of measurement sharing one breath. A turnout shows what an institution can still gather for a public occasion; emptying churches describe ordinary weeks over years. Influence can survive a decline in observance, and one Mass crowd does not by itself show observance returning.

items.title: Athens Blast Believed to Come From a Major Gas Leak, Mayor Says
items.body: A blast in Athens on Friday is believed to have been caused by a major gas leak, Athens Mayor Haris Doukas said, according to PBS. Neighbouring buildings were damaged and evacuated. The mayor's account states a suspected cause rather than a confirmed one.

sources.title: In UN address, Anand takes jab at 'great powers' disrupting global order

items.title: Canada Puts 'Strategic Autonomy' at the Front of Its UN Address
items.body: Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand placed “strategic autonomy” at the forefront of Canada's address to the United Nations General Assembly, CBC reports — a three-word phrase doing a lot of work in a chamber built for collective action. The setting is what makes the framing interesting. A general assembly speech is normally where a country talks about the rules it shares with others; here the emphasis lands on Canada's own room to manoeuvre. Autonomy from whom, and on which files — procurement, trade, defence — is the part the phrase leaves open, and it is the part that will be judged later by budgets rather than by speeches.

sources.title: Iran sticks to Hormuz plan after Trump rejects it

discussion.body: A public rejection is still a rejection. Insisting on a formal note is a way to keep a plan alive on a technicality while everyone can see the answer already given.
Or it's a deliberate refusal to treat a press remark as a decision — which keeps the option open for a formal deal later, and costs nothing in the meantime.
Either reading ends in the same place: the plan stays formally pending, and the Strait stays a subject of negotiation rather than a settled no.

items.title: Iran Waits for a Formal Rejection It Says Hasn't Arrived
items.body: Iranian officials say they are aware of President Trump's comments rejecting their new proposal, but that no formal message rejecting the plan — one that would open the Strait of Hormuz — has reached them, according to Deutsche Welle. That gap between a public remark and a delivered message is carrying real weight. Treating a presidential statement as a signal rather than a decision lets Tehran keep the plan on the table without appearing to defy Washington outright, and it preserves the possibility that the same proposal could be picked up again through a normal channel. Whether this is procedural stubbornness or deliberate negotiating room, the practical effect is the same: nothing is formally closed.

sources.title: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Review: The King of the Monsters Returns with a Direct Sequel That’s One Better Than the Last Movie in Almost Every Way

discussion.body: It is easy to read 'melodrama' as a put-down. Here it sits alongside the fights rather than against them — as if the emotional register and the spectacle are the same instrument.
Or it is a hedge. Grand feeling is one claim; two monsters leveling a city is another. The review's enthusiasm is for the staging, and staging is not the same as earned emotion.
Then the wager is that scale can carry feeling on its own — that a big enough image does the work quieter scenes would otherwise have to do.

items.title: The New Godzilla, Reviewed as an IMAX-Sized Melodrama
items.body: IndieWire's reviewer frames the new Godzilla film around its centrepiece bout: Godzilla squares off against King Ghidorah, and the fight arrives inside what the review calls an IMAX-sized melodrama — one it says features some of the most thrilling kaiju fights ever put on screen. That last part is a critic's superlative, not a measurement, but it is a clear one: the fights are the reason to be there, staged at the biggest scale available to them.

sources.title: Inside NYFF’s Buzzy Opening Night with James Gray’s ‘Paper Tiger’

items.title: Paper Tiger Played Well for the NYFF Crowd; the After-Party Talked Oscars
items.body: Neon's Paper Tiger played well for the Lincoln Center crowd on New York Film Festival opening night, IndieWire reports, and the conversation didn't stop at the credits: guests at the Tavern on the Green after-party debated the film's Oscar odds. After-party awards chatter says more about the mood of a room than about the race months ahead, but a crowd that spends the evening on a film's odds is at least a crowd that thinks it has a contender.

discussion.body: At least the movie version is honest about being a story. You buy a ticket knowing somebody made it up.
Nostalgia for a 'simpler' time is also made up. It just skips the credits, which is why it's harder to argue with.

items.title: The American West Offers Two Doors, and Neither Opens on the Present
items.body: Aeon Video's piece on the allure of the American West names two ways in: movie mythos, and nostalgia for a 'simpler' time. It calls the pull undeniable, and it is — but the two doors lead to very different rooms. One is openly a production, with a score and a horizon line composed for the camera. The other pretends nobody built it. My suspicion is that the second is the more powerful fiction, because it doesn't announce itself as one.
